scenes.visual: electron flow pumps H+ out; H+ flood back through ATP synthase
scenes.narration: This is the single most important idea in the chapter, so hold on to it. Electron flow and ATP synthesis are two separate events linked only by a proton gradient. On the left, electrons hop downhill through carriers in the inner membrane, and each exergonic step does work by pushing protons from the matrix out into the intermembrane space. That accumulation of protons is potential energy, like water behind a dam. On the right, ATP synthase lets those protons flood back down their gradient, and that flow drives the phosphorylation of ADP. Peter Mitchell proposed this in 1961, was met with deep skepticism and won the Nobel Prize for being right.

scenes.narration: Let me show you why electrons move at all. Every carrier has a reduction potential, plotted here on the vertical axis. NADH sits high, at a very negative potential, meaning it holds electrons loosely and donates them readily. Oxygen sits at the bottom, strongly positive, meaning it grabs electrons hungrily. Electrons always flow from low potential to high potential, from generous donor to greedy acceptor, and that is why they cascade from NADH down to oxygen. The total drop is about 1.14 volts, which translates to roughly minus 220 kilojoules per mole. That released energy is exactly what gets spent pumping protons across the membrane.

scenes.visual: complex I, III, IV pump; complex II feeder does not
scenes.narration: Now, we assemble the chain from named parts. Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, NADH-Q oxidoreductase, and are handed to ubiquinone. Complex III, Q-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, passes them to cytochrome c. Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, delivers them to oxygen. Those three are the proton pumps. Notice the side door. Complex II, succinate-Q reductase, feeds electrons from succinate-derived FADH2 into the Q pool, but it does not pump protons. That single fact, that Complex II is a feeder and not a pump, explains why FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH. The reduction potentials on the left confirm every step runs downhill.
scenes.slideTitle: The Respiratory Chain: Three Pumps Plus a Feeder
scenes.notes: Now we assemble the chain from named parts. Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I, NADH-Q oxidoreductase, and are handed to ubiquinone. Complex III, Q-cytochrome c oxidoreductase, passes them to cytochrome c. Complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase, delivers them to oxygen. Those three are the proton pumps. Notice the side door: Complex II, succinate-Q reductase, feeds electrons from succinate-derived FADH2 into the Q pool, but it does not pump protons. That single fact — Complex II feeds electrons into the Q pool but was never built with the proton-pumping subunits Complexes I, III, and IV carry — explains why FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH. The reduction potentials on the left confirm every step runs downhill.

scenes.visual: block the chain: upstream reduced, downstream oxidized
scenes.narration: This is a beautiful piece of experimental logic, and it is a favorite exam scenario, so reason through it with me. If you block the chain at one point, everything upstream of the block piles up in the reduced state because electrons cannot leave, and everything downstream becomes oxidized because no new electrons arrive. So rotenone, blocking Complex I, leaves NADH reduced and the rest oxidized. Antimycin A, blocking Complex III, leaves carriers up to cytochrome b reduced. Cyanide, blocking Complex IV, leaves the entire chain reduced and only oxygen unreduced. By reading which carriers turn reduced versus oxidized, you can deduce the exact sequence of electron flow.

scenes.visual: battery: charging, discharging, cut cable, uncoupler
scenes.narration: Tie the whole chapter together with one image, the mitochondrion as a rechargeable battery. The electron-transport chain is the charging cable, using the energy of electron flow to pump protons and build up charge, the proton-motive force, across the inner membrane. ATP synthase is the discharge circuit, letting protons flow back down to do useful work and make ATP. Now the diseases and drugs make sense. Cut the charging cable as cyanide does by blocking Complex IV and the battery never charges. Add an uncoupler, which pokes holes in the membrane, and the battery short-circuits, draining its charge as heat instead of ATP.
